relationship: water flows outward from the Lord's restored dwelling
rationale: Zechariah promises water going out from Jerusalem. Joel likewise describes Judah's flowing water outlets and a spring from the Lord's house watering a wadi. The outward flow from the sacred center connects the restoration pictures, without equating the wadi with Zechariah's seas.
source_text: On that day living water will go out from Jerusalem, half into the first sea and half into the last sea; it will be so in summer and spring.

target_units.text: On that day mountains will drip sweetness, hills will flow with milk, and all Judah’s water outlets will flow with water. A spring will come out of the Lord’s house and water the Wadi of Rushes.

relationship: the confession that the Lord is one
rationale: Zechariah's universal-kingship promise says that the Lord will be one and His name one. Deuteronomy's address to Israel likewise confesses that the Lord our God is one. The explicit confession is shared within their different settings.
source_text: The Lord will be king over all the earth. On that day the Lord will be one, and His name one,

target_units.text: And these are the ordinances and judgments which the Lord commanded the sons of Israel in the wilderness, when they came forth out of the land of Egypt: Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.

relationship: the Lord's kingship over all the earth and nations
rationale: Zechariah announces the Lord as king over all the earth. The psalm likewise calls God king of all the earth and says He reigns over the nations. The scope of His kingship directly corresponds.
source_text: The Lord will be king over all the earth. On that day the Lord will be one, and His name one,

target_units.text: For God is King of all the earth; make music with understanding.
God reigned over the nations; God sits upon His holy throne.

relationship: restored Jerusalem described through measured boundaries and named gates
rationale: Zechariah describes the land and Jerusalem's established places through named gates and a tower. Jeremiah likewise promises a rebuilt city bounded by a named tower, the Corner Gate and further measurements, ending with lasting sanctuary status. Both map restoration through city boundaries; the distinct tower and place names are not normalized into one list.
source_text: encircling all the land and the wilderness from Gabe to Remmon south of Jerusalem. Rama will remain in its place, from Benjamin’s Gate to the place of the First Gate, to the Gate of Corners and to Ananeel’s Tower, to the king’s wine vats.

target_units.text: Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and a city will be built for the Lord from Hanamel’s tower to the Corner Gate.
And its measurement will go out opposite them as far as Gareb’s hills, and it will be enclosed all around with chosen stones.
And all Asaremoth as far as the Kidron wadi, to the corner of the eastern Horse Gate, will be a sanctuary for the Lord. It will certainly never disappear or be torn down for ever.

relationship: secure inhabitation after destruction has ceased
rationale: Zechariah promises Jerusalem's confident dwelling with nothing accursed remaining. Isaiah likewise promises no more injustice, destruction or misery within the city's land and borders, with walls called Salvation. Both describe secure life after destructive conditions are removed.
source_text: They will dwell in her; there will no longer be anything accursed, and Jerusalem will dwell confidently.

target_units.text: Injustice will no longer be heard in your land, nor destruction and misery within your borders. Your walls will be called Salvation, and your gates Engraving.

relationship: confusion from the Lord turns opponents against their neighbors
rationale: Zechariah describes great bewilderment from the Lord and each man's hand grappling with his neighbor's. Samuel likewise reports terror from the Lord and a battle in which each man's sword is against his neighbor. The divinely caused confusion and internal fighting closely correspond.
source_text: On that day great bewilderment from the Lord will be upon them. Each will seize his neighbor’s hand, and his hand will grapple with his neighbor’s hand.

target_units.text: There was terror in the camp and in the field. All the people in the messab and the destroyers were terrified, and they were unwilling to act. The earth was astonished, and there was terror from the Lord.
Saul’s lookouts in Benjamin’s Geba saw the camp in turmoil this way and that.
Saul said to the people with him, “Please muster and see who has gone from you.” They mustered, and Jonathan and the one carrying his equipment could not be found.
Saul said to Ahijah, “Bring the ephoud near.” For he was bearing the ephoud before Israel that day.
While Saul spoke to the priest, the sound in the foreigners’ camp kept growing louder. Saul said to the priest, “Withdraw your hands.”
Saul and all the people with him cried out and came to the battle. Each man’s sword was against his neighbour, with exceedingly great confusion.

relationship: Judah gathers abundant spoils after the opposing forces fall
rationale: Zechariah announces Judah's battle and collection of surrounding peoples' gold, silver and clothing. Chronicles likewise describes Judah finding the defeated multitude and gathering abundant spoils and precious articles for three days. Both expressly portray Judah receiving extensive spoils from opponents.
source_text: Judah will draw up for battle in Jerusalem and gather the strength of all the surrounding peoples: gold, silver and clothing in very great abundance.

target_units.text: Judah reached the wilderness lookout and looked out and saw the multitude. There they were: all dead, fallen on the ground, with no survivor.

Jehoshaphat and his people came to plunder their spoils. They found many herds, baggage, spoils, and precious articles, and plundered them for themselves. They spent three days plundering the spoils, because they were so many.

relationship: judgment extends to horses, camels and other livestock
rationale: Zechariah's downfall reaches horses, mules, camels, donkeys and camp animals. Exodus likewise describes the Lord's hand bringing death to horses, beasts of burden, camels, cattle and sheep in Egypt. The overlapping animal list makes the extension of judgment particularly concrete.
source_text: This will also be the downfall of horses, mules, camels, donkeys and every animal in those camps, according to this downfall.

target_units.text: behold, the hand of the Lord shall be upon your livestock in the plains, upon the horses, and upon the beasts of burden, and upon the camels, and upon the cattle, and upon the sheep: an exceedingly great death.
At that time I will make a marvellous distinction between the Egyptians’ livestock and the sons of Israel’s livestock. Nothing belonging to the sons of Israel shall die.’”
God appointed a time, saying, “Tomorrow the Lord will do this in the land.”
The Lord did this the next day. All the Egyptians’ livestock died, but none of the sons of Israel’s livestock died.

relationship: the Festival of Tent-Pitching as worship directed to the Lord
rationale: Zechariah says survivors from the nations will annually worship the Lord and celebrate Tent-Pitching. Leviticus commands Israel's Feast of Tents for seven days with holy gatherings and offerings. The named festival connects the passages while Zechariah extends the described attendance to surviving nations.
source_text: Whoever remains from all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up each year to bow before the King, the Lord Almighty, and celebrate the Festival of Tent-Pitching.

target_units.text: Speak to the sons of Israel, saying: On the fifteenth day of this seventh month is the Feast of Tents unto the Lord for seven days.
And on the first day there shall be a holy convocation. You shall do no laborious work.

For seven days you shall bring whole burnt offerings unto the Lord. The eighth day shall be a holy convocation for you, and you shall bring whole burnt offerings unto the Lord. It is a closing observance; you shall do no laborious work.

relationship: required appearance before the Lord at the appointed festival
rationale: Zechariah warns about tribes that do not go to Jerusalem to bow before the King. Deuteronomy likewise commands regular appearance before the Lord at His chosen place, including the Feast of the Pitching of Tents. The obligation to attend connects them; no rainfall wording is added to Zechariah's warning.
source_text: Whoever among all the earth’s tribes does not go up to Jerusalem to bow before the King, the Lord Almighty—these will be added to those.

target_units.text: Three times in the year shall every male among you appear before the Lord your God, in the place which the Lord shall choose: in the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and in the Feast of Weeks, and in the Feast of the Pitching of Tents. You shall not appear before the Lord your God empty,

relationship: Egypt's worship of the Lord considered alongside His striking it
rationale: Zechariah warns Egypt of a divine blow if it does not attend the Lord's feast. Isaiah likewise describes Egyptians knowing the Lord and offering worship, and the Lord striking them before healing as they turn back. Both specifically place Egypt's relation to the Lord beside His punitive action, with different conditions and outcomes.
source_text: If Egypt’s tribe does not go up or come there, upon these too will be the downfall with which the Lord will strike all the nations that do not go up to celebrate the Festival of Tent-Pitching.

target_units.text: The Lord will be known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the Lord on that day. They will make sacrifices, vow vows to the Lord and pay them.
The Lord will strike the Egyptians with a great blow and heal them with healing. They will turn back to the Lord, and He will listen to them and heal them.

relationship: failure to keep the commanded Feast of Tents treated as wrongdoing
rationale: Zechariah names the refusal to go up for Tent-Pitching as Egypt's and the nations' sin. Deuteronomy explicitly commands keeping that feast and appearing before the Lord. The connection concerns the named observance and the requirement to keep it, while the addressed populations differ.
source_text: This will be Egypt’s sin and the sin of all the nations that do not go up to celebrate the Festival of Tent-Pitching.

target_units.text: You shall keep the Feast of Tents seven days, when you have gathered in from your threshing floor and from your winepress.

And you shall rejoice in your feast, you, and your son, and your daughter, and your male slave, and your female slave, and the Levite, and the sojourner, and the orphan, and the widow within your cities.

You shall keep a feast for seven days unto the Lord your God, in the place which the Lord your God shall choose for Himself; and if the Lord your God blesses you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, you shall rejoice.

Three times in the year shall every male among you appear before the Lord your God, in the place which the Lord shall choose: in the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and in the Feast of Weeks, and in the Feast of the Pitching of Tents. You shall not appear before the Lord your God empty,

relationship: objects associated with the sanctuary made holy to the Lord
rationale: Zechariah describes what is on a horse's bridle as holy and the Lord's-house cauldrons as like altar bowls. Exodus directs consecration of sanctuary furnishings and all their utensils as most holy. Both assign holiness to material objects; Zechariah's wider range is not reduced to the earlier furnishings.
source_text: On that day what is upon the horse’s bridle will be holy to the Lord Almighty, and the cauldrons in the Lord’s house will be like bowls before the altar.

target_units.text: With it anoint the Tent of Testimony and the ark of the testimony,
the lampstand and all its utensils, and the incense altar,
the altar of whole burnt offerings and all its utensils, the table and all its utensils, and the basin and its base.
Consecrate them, and they shall be most holy. Everyone who touches them shall be sanctified.

relationship: consecration extended across the vessels used in worship
rationale: Zechariah makes every cauldron in Jerusalem and Judah holy for those offering sacrifice. Exodus likewise consecrates the altar and table with all their utensils. The shared comprehensive holiness of vessels connects them, while Zechariah explicitly ranges beyond the sanctuary to the city and Judah.
source_text: Every cauldron in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the Lord Almighty. All who sacrifice will come, take some of them and boil in them. No Canaanite will remain in the house of the Lord Almighty on that day.

target_units.text: the altar of whole burnt offerings and all its utensils, the table and all its utensils, and the basin and its base.
Consecrate them, and they shall be most holy. Everyone who touches them shall be sanctified.

relationship: exclusion from the restored holy place
rationale: Zechariah ends with no Canaanite remaining in the Lord's house. Isaiah likewise promises that no uncircumcised and unclean person will again pass through holy Jerusalem. Both describe exclusion from the restored sacred place, while the differently named excluded groups are not equated.
source_text: Every cauldron in Jerusalem and Judah will be holy to the Lord Almighty. All who sacrifice will come, take some of them and boil in them. No Canaanite will remain in the house of the Lord Almighty on that day.

target_units.text: Awake, awake, Zion! Clothe yourself with your strength, Zion, and put on your glory, Jerusalem, holy city. No uncircumcised and unclean person will pass through you again.
